issues.legal_issue: Surplus land that vested in the State and was taken into possession before repeal remains with the State and does not qualify for restoration under the repeal legislation.
material_facts: The competent authority issued the vesting notification for the surplus land, and a notice directing its surrender was issued.
A possession certificate recorded that possession had been taken before the repeal legislation was enacted; a later order dismissing objections also recorded that possession had been taken.
The claimants sought the benefit of the repeal legislation on the basis that they remained in possession.
issues.conclusion: The claimants had no stateable claim under the repeal legislation because the land had vested in the State and possession had been taken before the repeal.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 10(3) and 10(5) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, and Section 3(2)(a) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, were considered in relation to vesting and possession. The Court held on the facts that the requisite actions under the 1976 Act had been completed before repeal; it did not need to decide whether possession in every case must be actual physical possession.

predicates.repeal_benefit_proceeding: A proceeding seeks relief under repeal legislation concerning surplus land.
predicates.state_vesting_occurred: The land vested in the State after the required vesting process was completed.
predicates.possession_taken_before_repeal: The State took possession of the land before the repeal legislation took effect.

issues.definition: When a proceeding seeks relief under repeal legislation and the land had vested in the State and been taken into its possession before repeal, the State retains the surplus land after repeal.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires surplus land after it has vested in the State cannot challenge alleged State inaction in taking possession, and the transfer is void.
material_facts: The land vested in the State following publication of the vesting notification.
The claimant asserted that it purchased the land from the former holders after that notification.
The claimant objected to the possession notice and later claimed entitlement to relief based on alleged continuing possession.
issues.conclusion: The post-vesting transfer was void ab initio, and the transferee was not entitled to challenge alleged inaction by the State in taking possession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Adarsh Seva Sahakari Ltd., Civil Appeal Nos. 369–370 of 2016, decided on 19 January 2016, for the principle that a transfer made after vesting is void ab initio and the transferee cannot challenge alleged State inaction in taking possession under Section 10(5) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976. The judgment identifies publication under Section 10(3) as the event upon which the surplus land vested in the State.

predicates.transferee_challenge_proceeding: A transferee brings a proceeding challenging the State's alleged failure to take possession of surplus land.
predicates.transfer_after_state_vesting: The land was transferred to the claimant after it had vested in the State.

issues.definition: If a transferee challenges alleged State inaction in a proceeding and acquired the land after State vesting, the transfer is void and the transferee cannot challenge that inaction.
